title: Danger, Brakes and Safety
summary: Early trains were exciting, but they could be dangerous: brakes were weak, signals were simple and workers got hurt joining wagons together. After some terrible accidents, clever inventors created air brakes, automatic couplers and signal boxes that stopped mistakes. Today trains are one of the safest ways to travel, thanks to the lessons learned long ago.

sections.heading: Fast, Heavy and Hard to Stop
paragraphs: Here is a simple experiment you can try in your head. Imagine pushing an empty shopping trolley and then letting go. It rolls a little and stops. Now imagine a trolley loaded with bricks. Once it is moving, it is much harder to stop. A railway train is that loaded trolley multiplied thousands of times. A Victorian express might weigh well over 100 tonnes; a long freight train could weigh many hundreds of tonnes. The same low friction that lets a train glide so easily along steel rails also means it needs a very long distance to stop. Steel wheels on steel rails do not grip like rubber tyres on a road.

On the earliest railways, the brakes were feeble. The locomotive had a brake, and the tender often had a hand brake turned by a wheel. Some carriages and wagons had brake vans, where a guard or brakeman turned a big wheel to press wooden or iron blocks against the wheels. On a long train, the driver had to whistle a signal and hope the brakemen heard it and acted in time. Each brake was worked separately, by a different person, so stopping a fast train could take a frighteningly long distance.

In America, many freight trains had brakes that could only be applied from wheels on top of each car. Brakemen had to climb up and run along the roofs of moving wagons, jumping from car to car, in rain, snow and darkness, turning each brake wheel in turn. It was so dangerous that brakemen were killed or badly hurt in large numbers every year, and it limited how long a train could safely be.

There were other dangers too. Steam locomotive boilers held water and steam under great pressure. If the metal was weak, the water ran too low, or someone tied down the safety valve, a boiler could burst with enormous force. Bridges built of cast iron, which is strong when squeezed but can snap when bent or shaken, sometimes failed. And there was the everyday risk of collisions, when one train ran into another that was stopped or moving more slowly ahead.

In the early days, trains on the same line were kept apart mainly by time. Railway policemen stood at intervals along the track with watches. If a train had passed less than a set number of minutes ago, they would signal the next train to slow down or stop; if more time had passed, they would wave it on. The trouble was obvious: the policeman had no idea whether the first train had actually got safely ahead, or had broken down just around the next bend. Accidents caused by this 'time interval' system were common.

Over the following 70 years, railways would solve these problems one by one, with better brakes, couplers, signals, bridges and rules. Sadly, many of the improvements only came after disasters showed, in the hardest possible way, what could go wrong. To understand why our trains are so safe today, we need to visit some of those dark days, calmly and respectfully, and see what people learned.

sections.heading: The Night the Tay Bridge Fell
paragraphs: The River Tay in eastern Scotland is wide and windy where it meets the sea near the city of Dundee. For years, travellers going north had to cross it by ferry. Then, in 1878, the North British Railway opened a new bridge, designed by the engineer Thomas Bouch. It was one of the longest bridges in the world, a slender line of iron lattice girders standing on iron piers, stretching about two miles across the water. Its tallest section, called the 'high girders', let ships pass underneath. The bridge opened to passengers on 1 June 1878, and Bouch was knighted for his achievement.

On the evening of Sunday 28 December 1879, a violent storm swept down the Tay. The wind was blowing almost straight across the bridge, at gale or even hurricane strength. At around 7:15 in the evening, a passenger train from Burntisland to Dundee, with a locomotive, five carriages and a luggage van, steamed out onto the bridge. Watchers on the shore saw its lights moving through the darkness, then a flash of sparks, and then nothing. The high girders had collapsed, and the whole train had fallen into the river.

There were no survivors. Because the exact number of passengers was never certain, historians give slightly different figures: 59 people are known to have died, and the total may have been as high as about 75. Only 46 bodies were ever recovered. It remains one of the worst railway disasters in British history.

A Court of Inquiry examined what had gone wrong, and its findings shocked the engineering world. Bouch had made no proper allowance for the pressure of strong wind on the bridge and on a train crossing it. The cross-bracing that was meant to stop the piers from swaying was too weak, and the small iron tabs, called lugs, that held the bracing were cast as part of the iron columns and could crack. Workers at the foundry had used poor-quality castings and sometimes filled defects instead of rejecting faulty parts. Maintenance had been poor, with loose tie bars rattling as trains passed. Some witnesses said trains often went faster than the bridge's speed limit of 25 mph.

The official report blamed the collapse on the gale overwhelming badly designed and badly made bracing. One member of the inquiry, Henry Rothery, wrote a separate report that placed the blame mainly on Bouch. Bouch's reputation was ruined, and he died less than a year later. His design for a great railway bridge across the Firth of Forth, near Edinburgh, was abandoned, and a completely new, much stronger design was chosen instead.

The disaster changed engineering rules. Bridge designers in Britain now had to calculate wind loads carefully, allowing for winds pushing with up to 56 pounds on every square foot of surface. A new, sturdier Tay Bridge was built right beside the stumps of the old one and opened in 1887; you can still see the old piers poking out of the water today. Remarkably, the locomotive was later hauled out of the river, repaired and put back to work, and railwaymen nicknamed it 'The Diver'. It kept running until 1919.

sections.heading: Armagh, 1889: Why Brakes Must Work by Themselves
paragraphs: Ten years after the Tay Bridge fell, an accident in Ireland showed that weak brakes could be just as deadly as weak bridges. On the morning of 12 June 1889, the Methodist Sunday school in Armagh, now in Northern Ireland, ran a day trip to the seaside town of Warrenpoint. Families and children were excited; tickets sold well. In the end, about 940 people squeezed into a train of 15 carriages run by the Great Northern Railway of Ireland.

Soon after leaving Armagh, the line climbed a steep hill. The locomotive was not powerful enough for such a heavy train, and the train stalled near the top. The crew decided to split the train in two: they would take the front part over the top, leave it at the next station, and come back for the rest. That meant uncoupling the rear ten carriages and leaving them standing on the steep slope.

Here is where the brakes mattered. The train had a vacuum brake, a system in which the brakes were worked by sucking air out of a pipe that ran the length of the train. But this was a 'simple', non-automatic vacuum brake. When the pipe was disconnected, the brakes on the rear carriages did not come on by themselves. The only thing holding those ten crowded carriages was the hand brake in the guard's van, helped by some stones placed behind the wheels. When the front part of the train was moved, it bumped the rear part slightly. The rear carriages began to roll backwards down the hill, faster and faster, and crashed into the next train coming up the line behind them.

Eighty people died and around 260 were injured. About a third of those killed were children. It was the worst railway accident in Ireland's history and the deadliest railway accident anywhere in the United Kingdom in the 19th century. The inquiry blamed the lack of brake power on the rear carriages, the decision to divide the train on a slope, the use of an engine that was too weak for the load and the inexperience of the driver.

This time the government acted fast. Within about two months, Parliament passed the Regulation of Railways Act 1889. It gave the Board of Trade, the government department that inspected railways, the power to order railway companies to fit three key safety measures to passenger lines. First, continuous automatic brakes: brakes on every carriage, controlled by the driver, that would come on by themselves if the train split apart. Second, the block system of signalling, so only one train could be in each section of line at a time. Third, interlocking of points and signals, so that a signalman could not set up a dangerous route. Many historians see this law as the start of modern railway safety in Britain.

The key word was 'automatic'. A brake that only worked when everything went right was not good enough. Railways needed brakes that switched themselves on when something went wrong. An American inventor had already shown how to do it.

sections.heading: George Westinghouse and the Brake That Fails Safe
paragraphs: George Westinghouse was born on 6 October 1846 in Central Bridge, New York, the son of a man who made farm machinery. As a teenager he served in the American Civil War, first in the Union army and then as an engineer in the navy. After the war he started inventing, and one day, the story goes, he was travelling by train when his journey was held up by a wreck ahead: two trains had run into each other on the same track. Their drivers had seen each other coming, but with hand brakes there was no way to stop in time. Westinghouse decided there must be a better way.

His answer was to use compressed air, air squeezed into a small space so it pushes hard to escape. In 1869, at the age of just 22, he demonstrated his air brake in Pittsburgh and received his first patent for it on 13 April 1869. That same year he founded the Westinghouse Air Brake Company. In his first system, called a 'straight air' brake, a pump on the locomotive squeezed air into a tank, and when the driver opened a valve, the compressed air flowed down a pipe along the train into brake cylinders on every car. Each cylinder pushed a piston that pressed brake shoes against the wheels. For the first time, the driver could apply the brakes on the whole train at once.

But there was a dangerous weakness. If a hose burst, or the train broke apart, the air escaped and the brakes simply did not work. Westinghouse realised the system needed to be turned upside down. In 1872 he introduced his automatic air brake, and it is one of the cleverest safety ideas in railway history.

Here is how it works. A pipe, called the brake pipe, runs the whole length of the train and is kept filled with compressed air. Under each car there is a reservoir, a small air tank, and a clever valve called the triple valve. While the brake pipe is at full pressure, the triple valve lets air flow into the reservoir to fill it up and keeps the brakes off. When the driver wants to slow down, he lets some air out of the brake pipe. The pressure drops, and each triple valve responds by letting air from its own reservoir into its brake cylinder, putting the brakes on. To release the brakes, the driver raises the pipe pressure again.

Now think about what happens if the train accidentally splits apart, or a hose bursts. The brake pipe loses all its pressure in an instant. Every triple valve sees the drop and applies the brakes as hard as possible, using the air already stored on each car. The broken train stops itself. Engineers call this 'fail-safe': when something goes wrong, the system falls into the safe condition, not the dangerous one. That is exactly what the rear carriages at Armagh had lacked.

Westinghouse's automatic air brake, improved many times over the years, was adopted on railways almost everywhere. Some British railways preferred an automatic vacuum brake, which works on the same fail-safe idea but uses suction instead of pressure; Britain's railways switched over to air brakes in the diesel age of the 1960s. Westinghouse went on to receive about 360 patents in his lifetime. In 1881 he founded the Union Switch and Signal Company to make railway signals and switches, and later he became famous for promoting alternating-current electricity. But the air brake, which let trains become longer, faster and far safer, was the invention that made his name.

sections.heading: Fingers, Pins and Janney's Knuckle
paragraphs: Brakes were not the only deadly problem, especially on American freight lines. Every time wagons were joined together, someone had to do it by hand. For much of the 1800s, most American cars used a link-and-pin coupler. Each car had a socket at the end. To couple two cars, a brakeman stood between them, held a heavy iron link in one socket, and waited as the engine pushed the cars together, guiding the link into the other socket and then dropping an iron pin through to lock it.

If the brakeman's timing was a fraction of a second off, his hand could be crushed between the cars. If he slipped, he could fall beneath the wheels. Railroad workers sometimes said you could tell an experienced brakeman by his missing fingers. Between 1877 and 1887, about 38 per cent of accidents to American railway workers involved coupling cars. In the 1880s, working on the railroad was one of the most dangerous jobs in the country.

The solution came from Eli Janney, a Virginian who had served as an officer in the Confederate army during the Civil War and later worked as a clerk in a dry goods store in Alexandria, Virginia. Legend says he worked out his idea by whittling wooden models during his lunch breaks. Whether or not that is exactly true, in 1873 he received a US patent for a new kind of automatic coupler.

Janney's coupler works a bit like two hands clasping. On the end of each car is a hinged metal jaw called a knuckle. When two cars are pushed together, the open knuckles meet, swing shut around each other and lock automatically with a pin that drops into place. Nobody has to stand between the cars. To uncouple, a worker pulls a lever, called a cut lever, from the side of the car, which lifts the locking pin and lets the knuckles open. The worker never needs to step into the deadly gap.

Adoption was slow at first, because many different couplers were being invented and railroads did not want to buy expensive new equipment. In 1888 the Master Car Builders' Association, a group of railway engineers, chose a slightly modified version of Janney's design as the standard shape, so that couplers made by different companies would always fit together. That kind of agreement on a shared standard is one of the quiet heroes of railway history.

Even so, railroads moved slowly until the law pushed them. A former Iowa railroad commissioner named Lorenzo Coffin spent years travelling, writing and lobbying, almost single-handedly, to force the railroads to change. Finally, on 2 March 1893, in the last days of President Benjamin Harrison's term, Congress passed the Safety Appliance Act. It required trains to have power brakes, such as air brakes, so the driver could control the train's speed without brakemen running on roofs, and automatic couplers that joined on impact without anyone going between the cars. It also required secure grab irons, the handholds on the ends and sides of cars. Railroads were given a grace period, and the law came fully into force in 1900. The results were dramatic. Coupling accidents fell from 11,710 in 1893 to 2,256 in 1902, even though there were more trains running. Knuckle couplers based on Janney's design are still used on freight trains in North America today.

sections.heading: Signal Boxes, Blocks and Clever Levers
paragraphs: Strong brakes help a train stop. But the best accident is the one that never starts, and that is the job of signalling. Remember the old 'time interval' system, where a policeman with a watch could only guess whether the line ahead was clear. The electric telegraph, which we met sending time signals along the line, offered something far better.

With the telegraph, a railway could be divided into sections called blocks, with a signalman at each end. When a train left one block and entered the next, the signalman ahead could send a message back by bell code saying 'train out of section'. Only then would the signalman behind let another train into that block. This is the absolute block system: never more than one train in a section at a time. It is based on distance, not time, so a broken-down train is always protected, because the next train simply is not allowed in. The block system spread across British railways during the 1850s and 1860s and was made compulsory on passenger lines by the 1889 Act.

Signals themselves changed too. Early railways used flags, lamps, boards and balls hoisted on poles. By the 1840s, semaphore signals, with a moving arm on a tall post, were appearing: arm straight out meant stop, arm lowered meant go, with coloured lamps for night. Signals were worked by levers in a small building beside the track, the signal box, connected to the signals and points by long wires and metal rods.

Even with a block system, a signalman could make a mistake. He might set the points to send a train into a siding while showing a 'clear' signal for the main line, or clear signals for two trains whose paths would cross. The cure was interlocking. An early form appeared at Bricklayers Arms Junction in south London in 1843, and in 1856 the engineer John Saxby patented an improved system. In an interlocking frame, the levers are linked underneath by a grid of sliding metal bars. Pull one lever, and its bar slides across and physically blocks any lever that would set up a conflicting route. A signal for a route simply cannot be cleared until the points for that route are set correctly. It is a mechanical puzzle that makes the most dangerous mistakes impossible. Interlocking became so popular that by 1873 the London and North Western Railway alone had about 13,000 interlocked levers.

Weather taught another lesson. On 21 January 1876, during a blizzard at Abbots Ripton in Huntingdonshire, England, the Flying Scotsman express from Edinburgh ran past signals that were showing 'clear' even though the signalman had set them to danger: snow and ice had stuck the semaphore arms and their wires. The express hit a coal train, and a second express then ran into the wreckage. Thirteen people died. Afterwards, railways changed their practice so that signals normally rested at danger and were only cleared when a train was expected, and the Great Northern Railway introduced a new 'somersault' signal arm, pivoted in the middle so snow could not easily jam it.

Little by little, a thinking machine was being built around the trains: blocks, bells, interlocked levers and fail-safe brakes. Each piece was designed so that if a person slipped up or a part failed, the system would stop trains rather than send them into danger.

sections.heading: Lives on the Line: Workers, Unions and the Pullman Strike
paragraphs: Behind every train were the people who ran it: drivers and firemen on the footplate, guards and brakemen, signalmen, track workers, shunters and station staff. Their work was hard and often dangerous. Shifts were very long, sometimes far more than 12 hours, and tired workers make mistakes. Pay could be cut whenever business was bad, and an injured worker might lose his job with little or no help.

To protect themselves, railway workers formed some of the earliest big trade unions, groups of workers who bargain together with employers. In the United States, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers was founded in 1863, followed by unions for firemen, conductors and trainmen. In 1877, after wage cuts, railroad workers walked off the job in what became known as the Great Railroad Strike, spreading from West Virginia to many cities. It was put down with the help of soldiers and armed militias, and many people were killed.

The most famous railway strike of the century began in 1894 in Pullman, a company town on the edge of Chicago built by George Pullman, maker of luxury sleeping cars. Pullman's workers lived in houses owned by the company and paid rent to the company. When trade slumped in 1893 and 1894, the company cut wages by roughly a quarter or more, but did not lower the rents. On 11 May 1894, about 4,000 Pullman factory workers went on strike.

They were supported by the American Railway Union, a new union led by Eugene V. Debs, which was open to all kinds of railway workers rather than just one trade. From 26 June, union members across the country refused to handle any train that included a Pullman car. At its height, around 250,000 workers in 27 states took part, and much of the nation's railway traffic, especially in the West, came to a halt.

The railroad companies and the federal government fought back. Courts issued an injunction, a legal order, banning the union from interfering with trains carrying the US mail. President Grover Cleveland sent about 12,000 army troops to Chicago in early July, even though the Governor of Illinois objected. There was rioting, burning of railway cars and violence, and dozens of people were killed. The strike collapsed by 20 July 1894. Debs was jailed for six months for disobeying the court order, and the American Railway Union fell apart. Only days before the troops arrived, Cleveland had signed a law making Labor Day a national holiday in the United States, on 28 June 1894.

Workers' campaigns did slowly bring change. In 1907, the United States passed the Hours of Service Act, which limited how long train crews could be made to work without rest, usually to 16 hours at a time. Safety laws, unions and better machines together made railway work less deadly in the 20th century, although it remained a tough job.

So far we have looked at the railway from the dangerous end: the footplate, the signal box and the gap between two wagons. But most people who rode the trains never saw any of that. They sat in a carriage, watched fields flash by, and found that their whole lives were changing. In the next part, we will step off the footplate and into a passenger carriage, to see how railways transformed food, holidays, newspapers, cities and everyday life.

deepDive: Railway safety history is a classic example of what engineers call learning from failure. Early railways relied on human vigilance: watchmen timing trains, brakemen turning wheels, signalmen remembering which points were set. Accidents revealed that any system depending on people never making a mistake would eventually fail. The great inventions of this period all replace vigilance with design. Westinghouse's automatic air brake (patented in 1869, with the automatic triple-valve version in 1872) makes loss of pressure apply the brakes, so a broken pipe or a divided train stops itself. Interlocking frames make conflicting signal settings physically impossible. The absolute block system replaces time intervals with space intervals, so a stopped train is protected however long it stands. Janney's knuckle coupler removes the need to stand between moving cars. Historians also debate why change was so slow. Railway companies argued that new brakes and couplers were costly, that rival designs were not yet proven, and that standards were needed before investing. Many reforms therefore came only after high-profile disasters and long campaigns: the 1889 Regulation of Railways Act followed Armagh within about two months, while the US Safety Appliance Act of 1893 followed years of lobbying by Lorenzo Coffin and gave railroads until 1900 to comply. The numbers show the effect: US coupling accidents fell from 11,710 in 1893 to 2,256 in 1902. The Tay Bridge disaster raises a different question, about engineering knowledge. Bouch was not simply careless; wind loading on large structures was poorly understood, and he relied on earlier advice. Yet the inquiry also found poor castings and supervision. Modern analyses have argued about how much each factor mattered, and some researchers have suggested the bridge may have been weakened by fatigue or by fast trains before the storm. Death tolls are also uncertain: 59 known victims, perhaps up to about 75, because no exact passenger list existed. Similarly, death figures for the 1894 Pullman Strike vary between sources. Good history keeps these uncertainties visible rather than choosing the most dramatic number.
funFact: The locomotive that plunged into the River Tay in the 1879 bridge disaster was hauled out of the water, repaired and kept working for about 40 more years, earning the nickname 'The Diver'.
